title: Colossians 2:16–23
context: Because the debt is canceled and the powers disarmed in Christ, Paul frees the church from judgmental pressure over food, drink, festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths—shadows whose substance belongs to Christ. He warns against disqualification through ascetic show, angel worship, and vision-boasting that fails to hold the Head, and against elemental regulations that look wise but cannot restrain the flesh.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: On because the debt is canceled and the powers disarmed in Christ, a few classic voices from each tradition.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Therefore - Seeing these things are so. Let none judge you - That is, regard none who judge you. In meat or drink - For not observing the ceremonial law in these or any other particulars. Or in respect of a yearly feast, the new moon, or the weekly Jewish sabbaths.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Col 2:16–23)

reformed.quote: What he had previously said of circumcision he now extends to the difference of meats and days. For circumcision was the first introduction to the observance of the law, other things followed afterwards. To judge means here, to hold one to be guilty of a crime, or to impose a scruple of conscience, so that we are no longer free.

verses.text: Let no one therefore judge you in eating or drinking, or with respect to a feast day or a new moon or a Sabbath day,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Therefore” looks back to the cross’s cancelation and triumph. No one may reinstate a courtroom over meals and calendar days as if those ruled the conscience.

Christ frees believers from human religious verdicts that add shadows as terms of acceptance. Grace invites a clean conscience before God, not anxiety under food-and-festival judges.
verses.reformedNotes:
Judgment over diet and sacred days is ruled out by what God has already done in Christ. The church must not let shadow-keepers become the bench.

Christian liberty here is gospel liberty. Belonging is settled at the cross, so ceremonial scorekeeping cannot reopen the case.

verses.text: which are a shadow of the things to come; but the body is Christ’s.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shadows had a pointing role; they were never the destination. The substance—the solid body—belongs to Christ.

Classical Arminians gladly keep Christ at the center: ceremonies may teach, but they must not replace the Savior to whom they pointed. Faith rests in Him, not in the silhouette.
verses.reformedNotes:
Paul’s shadow/substance contrast protects the sufficiency of Christ. Old-covenant patterns anticipated; they do not complete what the Son fulfills.

Chasing the shadow after the substance has come is a category mistake. Christ is the reality; calendars and menus are not rivals to Him.

verses.text: Let no one rob you of your prize by self-abasement and worshiping of the angels, dwelling in the things which he has not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,
verses.arminianNotes:
Another threat: spiritual showmanship—harsh treatment of the body, angel mediation, vision tours that inflate the ego while claiming humility.

Such religion can genuinely mislead and disqualify in the sense of cheating believers of their prize by false standards. Grace calls the church to refuse intimidation dressed as deeper piety.
verses.reformedNotes:
The opponents disqualify by insisting on extras: asceticism, angel worship, visionary detail. Pride hides under voluntary humility.

A sensuous mind can produce very religious talk. The danger is not too little spirituality but spirituality detached from Christ’s finished work.
verses.keyContrast: Both reject vision-and-ascetic elitism. Arminians stress the believer’s enabled duty to refuse disqualification; Reformed readers press that God keeps His people by holding them to Christ rather than to inflated spiritual hierarchies.

verses.text: and not holding firmly to the Head, from whom all the body, being supplied and knit together through the joints and ligaments, grows with God’s growth.
verses.arminianNotes:
The root failure is not holding the Head. Growth is God’s gift through Christ to a body, being supplied and knit together—not through private ladders around Jesus.

Stay fastened to Christ and to His people. Grace grows the body as members remain in the Head who supplies life.
verses.reformedNotes:
Sever the Head and the body starves, however impressive the angel talk. Growth that is from God flows from Christ through the church’s connections.

God grows His church by union with the Head. Healthy joints and ligaments matter because they channel life from Christ, not because technique replaces Him.

verses.text: If you died with Christ from the elemental spirits of the world, why, as though living in the world, do you subject yourselves to ordinances,
verses.arminianNotes:
Death with Christ ends elemental slavery. Returning to regulation-religion acts as if that death never happened.

Arminians press the incongruity: those who have died with Christ are called to live free from world-element bondage. Grace that united them to His death also summons a consistent walk.
verses.reformedNotes:
Union includes death to the elemental powers. Submission to their rulebook denies the new location believers already have in Christ.

Indicative first—you died with Christ—then the question that exposes relapse. Identity in the crucified Lord undercuts re-enslavement.

verses.arminianNotes:
Paul quotes the slogan-stack of restrictive religion. The phrases sound holy and urgent; they function as a new law of avoidance.

Not every “don’t” is godliness. Grace produces holiness from life in Christ, not from a lengthening list of untouchables that replace the gospel.
verses.reformedNotes:
The triple prohibition satirizes man-made severity. Handle, taste, touch—control by taboo.

Such commands often feel safer than faith in Christ. Paul exposes them as the world’s elementary grammar, not the Spirit’s way of holiness.

verses.text: (all of which perish with use), according to the precepts and doctrines of men?
verses.arminianNotes:
The objects of these rules perish with use. Building a righteousness system on perishable things, by human precepts, is a tragic misinvestment.

Human teachings can bind consciences tightly and still miss Christ. Believers are free—and responsible—to measure every precept by the Lord they received.
verses.reformedNotes:
Perishable things cannot carry eternal weight. “The precepts and doctrines of men” names the authority problem: man speaking where Christ has freed.

Doctrines of men may look careful while remaining earthbound. Only Christ’s word and work secure a holiness that outlasts what perishes with use.

verses.text: These things indeed appear like wisdom in self-imposed worship, humility, and severity to the body, but aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh.
verses.arminianNotes:
The final verdict: impressive packaging, empty power. Self-made religion, asceticism, and bodily severity look wise yet fail to stop fleshly indulgence.

Grace changes the heart in Christ; harsh religion often feeds pride while leaving appetite untouched. True wisdom stays with the Head, not with self-invented severity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Appearance of wisdom is not wisdom. Will-worship and severity can decorate the flesh rather than crucify it.

Reformed conclusion to the chapter’s warning: only union with the crucified and risen Christ restrains the flesh. Humanly invented religion cannot do what the gospel does.
verses.keyContrast: Both deny that ascetic self-made religion defeats the flesh. Arminians typically urge a grace-enabled turn from empty severity to life in Christ; Reformed readers typically insist that only God’s work in union with Christ—not human will-worship—actually breaks fleshly indulgence.
